series.blurb: On his first day at a new job, Luca has to give something to a Mr Rossi, and nobody seems to know who Mr Rossi is.
Luca has just moved to Via Verdi, and every day a stranger stands in the street and watches his house.
Money keeps vanishing from Sara's family home, and her little brother Tommaso is acting very strangely.
Luca's sister Anna finds a phone in the street, and the messages that keep arriving sound like a secret plan.
Giulia, a nurse, finds what looks like the perfect flatmate, but Marta comes home at four every morning and will not say where she goes.
Every morning at ten a quiet lady sits in Gino's bar and writes in a little book, and Piero cannot stop wondering what she writes.
In the little town of Spello, Elena keeps finding other people's things outside her bookshop each morning, and the neighbours start to wonder who is taking them.
Kate, a young Irish woman, spends a week in Bologna and gets by in Italian: a room, a dinner, a doctor, a lost phone and two new friends.
Davide has just moved to Turin and knows nobody. One errand at a time (the doctor, the bank, the post office, the barber, a call to his landlord) the city starts to feel like home.
A year of Italian traditions through the Moretti family of Bologna: Christmas and the Befana, Carnevale, Easter and Pasquetta, Ferragosto, and the weekly feast of Sunday lunch.
Over coffee at Gino's bar, Piero tells Elena the story of his life: a village by the sea, a red dress, a long silence.
Nonna Rita tells her granddaughter Chiara about growing up in a Puglia village in the 1960s: the one-room school, the family's olive trees, a first job, the first television and a boy with a chair.
Sofia and her boyfriend Matteo hunt for their first flat together in Milan, between impossible prices, a pushy agent and an offer that is too good to be true.
Irene and Pietro spend two weeks crossing Italy by train: Rome, Naples, Venice, Florence and Palermo, five real cities compared through history, art and food.
Five mismatched colleagues who lost every match last year have one month, and one stern woman from accounts, to become a five-a-side football team.
Piero takes the train back to his seaside village after a lifetime away, with his son, his grandson and Elena, to find his old friend Franco.
Alessandro is nearly thirty and bored of selling holidays he never takes, so he applies to an ice-cream company: an application, a phone call, two interviews and a nerve-racking first week.
On Sara's first week at a small publisher, the only copy of a secret new novel vanishes from the boss's desk, and she is the obvious suspect.

Giulia, thirty, records a weekly show from her bedroom about everyday life in Italy: phones, living with your parents, coffee, city versus countryside and cheap travel, with strong opinions and listeners' questions.
In her history lessons, the teacher Ms Ferri tells her class how Italy was made: Roman roads, Dante's language, Leonardo in Milan, the Unification and the great emigration.
Building work at Gino's bar uncovers a metal box hidden in a wall for sixty years, and the whole of Via Verdi sets out to deliver a letter that never arrived.

Five short magazine articles on debates that divide Italy today, each giving both sides: crowds in Venice, remote work and the return to the villages, local languages, slow food against fast food, and young people leaving for abroad.
A young journalist travels to a tiny island off Sicily in the dead of winter to find the ferry captain who has vanished, and discovers that a hundred islanders are all telling the same lie.

Nicola has moved to Melbourne, Valentina has stayed in Turin: five long emails between two old school friends about work, missing home, love, a father's illness and the question of whether to come back.

On the night train from Rome to Sicily a passenger vanishes from his cabin somewhere after Naples, and a retired schoolteacher and a young conductor have until the ferry docks to work out where he went.
Marta comes home from Milan to find her family's Bologna trattoria half empty and deep in debt, and has to save it without touching a single one of her father's recipes.
Five magazine pieces on the Italian language: the words it gave the world, its many local languages, its gestures, its false friends and the English words now flooding in.
A small painted Madonna vanishes from a Florentine church during building work, and a young restorer and the old sacristan have one day to find it before the police are called.
A newly qualified doctor takes over the practice in a snowbound village in Abruzzo, where an empty waiting room, a herb woman and a winter night decide whether she will ever belong.

Five true stories behind the Italian table: the tomato's slow welcome, the invention of espresso, how dried pasta conquered Naples, the cooking of the poor, and the snail from Bra that took on fast food.
Five ironic opinion columns by the same columnist on commuting, the vanishing corner shop, the cult of the aperitivo, working from home and the Sunday stroll.
Three estranged siblings inherit their mother's house in Liguria, along with a clause in her will that none of them understands and a notary who answers only in legal prose.
At a struggling local paper in Turin, a young reporter gets a tip about a school building contract and learns how little of a story survives once it has to be true.
In a provincial court in Emilia a widow stands trial for a fraud she says her late husband committed, and the court interpreter discovers that a single verb can tip the scales.
After hail and drought strike a family vineyard in the Langhe, a father and daughter clash over tradition and a changing climate while a courteous foreign buyer waits for an answer.
Five true portraits of Italians who changed their fields, each told through one revealing episode: Maria Montessori, Rita Levi-Montalcini, Enrico Fermi, Natalia Ginzburg and Adriano Olivetti.
A translator in Rome finds an unpublished nineteenth-century memoir hidden inside an old dictionary, and its grammar turns out to hold the key to a vanished girl.
One year in Venice told by five voices, a glassblower, a ferrywoman, a retired teacher, a tourist who stays and a child, linked by a crooked blue glass bird.
Five short reflective essays in the tradition of the Italian elzeviro: on slowness, translation, memory and places, silence and the art of conversation.
